title: Written and unwritten constitutions
examples: Does the UK have a written constitution?

explain.say: Some rule books are one thick book on a shelf. Others are a pile of notes, letters and habits everyone just follows. Countries are like that too. Look at the board: on the left, a constitution in one document; on the right, one spread across many places.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Both set the rules; they differ in form

explain.say: See the left side light up? Codified means collected into one main document. The USA, India, Japan, Nigeria and Brazil all have one. Changing it needs special votes, so rights stay steady. Can you see why that makes some people feel safe?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Both set the rules; they differ in form

explain.say: Now the right side. The UK, New Zealand and Israel have no single document. Their constitution is uncodified, which means spread across ordinary laws, court decisions and customs. Parliament can change much of it with a normal vote. Flexible, or risky?

explain.say: Here is where the UK's rules really live. Some are big laws, like Magna Carta from 1215. Some are court rulings. And some are customs, like the King signing every new law. Which box surprises you most?

explain.say: Fans of written constitutions say clear rules protect rights from a passing majority. Fans of uncodified ones say they adapt quickly. You compared like a real lawyer! Wow: the last British monarch to refuse to sign a law was Queen Anne, back in 1708.

faq.a: Codified means written down and collected into one main document. A codified constitution is the single top law of a country, like India's or the USA's.

faq.q: Does the UK have a constitution?
faq.a: Yes, but not in one document. Its constitution is uncodified: it comes from Acts of Parliament, court rulings, old documents like Magna Carta, and customs called conventions.
asks: Why does Britain have no written constitution?

faq.a: Here, a convention is an unwritten rule everyone follows by habit, like the monarch always agreeing to laws passed by parliament. Breaking one is not illegal but would cause a political storm.

faq.q: Which is better, written or unwritten?
faq.a: Each has strengths. Written constitutions are clear and hard to change, which protects rights. Uncodified ones are flexible but rely on leaders respecting traditions.
The UK, New Zealand and Israel are the best-known examples. Israel uses a set of Basic Laws instead of one document.

facts: Magna Carta was agreed in England in 1215 and parts of it are still law in England today.
